notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Irrigation is the artificial supply of water to agricultural land when rainfall is insufficient or unreliable.
  • It supplements natural rainfall.
  • Irrigation is essential in many parts of India because rainfall is:
  • Seasonal.
  • Unevenly distributed.
  • Variable from year to year.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Irrigation → Artificial Supply of Water to Crops

2. Importance of Irrigation

Irrigation helps:

  • Reduce monsoon dependence.
  • Increase crop yield.
  • Support multiple cropping.
  • Grow water-intensive crops.
  • Stabilise agricultural production.
  • Expand cultivation into dry regions.
3. Why India Needs Irrigation

Major reasons include:

  • Seasonal monsoon rainfall.
  • Uneven spatial distribution of rainfall.
  • Frequent droughts.
  • Long dry season in many regions.
  • High agricultural water demand.
  • Need for Rabi and summer cultivation.
4. Irrigation and Cropping Intensity
  • Reliable irrigation allows more than one crop to be grown on the same land in a year.
  • Therefore, irrigation usually increases cropping intensity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Irrigation ↑ → Cropping Intensity ↑

5. Irrigation and Agricultural Productivity

Irrigation improves productivity by:

  • Maintaining soil moisture.
  • Supporting timely sowing.
  • Improving fertiliser response.
  • Reducing crop stress.
  • Allowing HYV cultivation.
6. Major Sources of Irrigation in India

Important sources include:

  • Canals.
  • Wells.
  • Tube wells.
  • Tanks.
  • Reservoirs.
  • Lift irrigation.
  • Micro-irrigation.
7. Surface Irrigation

Surface irrigation uses water from sources such as:

  • Rivers.
  • Canals.
  • Tanks.
  • Reservoirs.
8. Groundwater Irrigation

Groundwater irrigation uses water obtained through:

  • Dug wells.
  • Tube wells.
  • Borewells.
9. Canal Irrigation
  • Canal irrigation supplies water through artificial channels.
  • Canals may divert water from:
  • Rivers.
  • Reservoirs.
  • Barrages.
10. Types of Canal Irrigation

Canals are broadly classified into:

  • Inundation canals.
  • Perennial canals.
11. Inundation Canal
  • Inundation canals receive water mainly when river levels rise during floods or high-flow periods.
  • They do not provide a reliable year-round supply.
12. Perennial Canal
  • Perennial canals receive regulated water from dams or barrages.
  • They can provide a more dependable supply throughout the agricultural season.
📌 Must-Memorise

Perennial Canal → Regulated Year-Round Supply

13. Regions Favourable for Canal Irrigation

Canal irrigation is especially suitable in:

  • Flat plains.
  • Perennial river basins.
  • Areas with extensive alluvial land.
14. Canal Irrigation in Northern Plains

Canals are important in:

  • Punjab.
  • Haryana.
  • Uttar Pradesh.
  • Rajasthan.

The level terrain facilitates canal construction.

15. Advantages of Canal Irrigation

Advantages include:

  • Large area coverage.
  • Reliable water from regulated rivers.
  • Support for intensive farming.
  • Possibility of multipurpose use.
16. Problems of Canal Irrigation

Poorly managed canals may cause:

  • Waterlogging.
  • Salinity.
  • Seepage.
  • Uneven water distribution.
  • Loss of cultivable land.
17. Waterlogging
  • Waterlogging occurs when the groundwater table rises close to the surface.
  • Roots receive insufficient oxygen.
  • Crop growth declines.
18. Salinity from Irrigation
  • Excess irrigation in dry areas can bring dissolved salts toward the surface.
  • Strong evaporation leaves salts behind.
  • Soil productivity declines.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Over-Irrigation → Waterlogging + Salinity

19. Well Irrigation
  • Wells draw groundwater from shallow aquifers.
  • Traditional dug wells are widely used in rural India.
  • Their success depends on:
  • Water table.
  • Aquifer conditions.
  • Recharge.
20. Tube-Well Irrigation
  • Tube wells tap deeper groundwater using pipes and pumps.
  • They can provide a large and regular water supply where aquifers are productive.
21. Areas Favourable for Tube Wells

Tube wells are especially successful in:

  • Ganga Plain.
  • Punjab.
  • Haryana.
  • Western Uttar Pradesh.
  • Bihar.

Deep alluvial aquifers favour groundwater extraction.

22. Advantages of Tube Wells
  • Farmer-controlled supply.
  • Water available when needed.
  • Limited conveyance loss.
  • Suitable for intensive farming.
23. Problems of Tube-Well Irrigation

Excessive use can cause:

  • Falling water table.
  • Increased pumping cost.
  • Land subsidence in extreme cases.
  • Water-quality deterioration.
24. Groundwater Depletion
  • Groundwater depletion occurs when extraction exceeds recharge over a long period.
  • Irrigation is a major driver in many agricultural regions.
25. Punjab-Haryana Groundwater Stress
  • Intensive rice-wheat farming has created high groundwater demand.
  • Paddy irrigation during the Kharif season places heavy pressure on aquifers.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

High Rainfall Crop in Semi-Arid Region → High Irrigation Demand

26. Tank Irrigation
  • Tanks are artificial or modified water-storage bodies.
  • They collect:
  • Rainfall runoff.
  • Stream flow.
  • Tank irrigation is especially important in Peninsular India.
27. Why Tank Irrigation is Common in Peninsular India

Reasons include:

  • Undulating terrain.
  • Hard-rock geology.
  • Seasonal streams.
  • Natural depressions.
  • Monsoon rainfall concentration.
28. Tank-Irrigation States

Tank irrigation is traditionally important in:

  • Tamil Nadu.
  • Andhra Pradesh.
  • Telangana.
  • Karnataka.
29. Eri System of Tamil Nadu
  • Traditional irrigation tanks in Tamil Nadu are called eris.
  • They store monsoon runoff.
  • Many are connected in cascades.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Eri → Traditional Tamil Nadu Irrigation Tank

30. Tank Cascade
  • A tank cascade is a chain of interconnected tanks.
  • Overflow from one tank may feed another downstream.
  • This improves local water utilisation.
31. Functions of Tamil Nadu Tanks

Eris provide:

  • Irrigation.
  • Groundwater recharge.
  • Flood moderation.
  • Livestock water.
  • Wetland habitat.
32. Problems of Tank Irrigation

Common problems include:

  • Siltation.
  • Encroachment.
  • Broken bunds.
  • Blocked channels.
  • Poor maintenance.
33. Tank Desiltation
  • Desilting removes accumulated sediment.
  • It can restore storage capacity.
  • The removed silt may sometimes improve nearby agricultural soils.
34. Lift Irrigation
  • Lift irrigation raises water from a lower level to a higher field using pumps.
  • It is used where gravity flow is not possible.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lift Irrigation → Water Pumped Upward

35. River-Lift Irrigation
  • Water may be pumped directly from rivers into canals or fields.
  • Energy cost is an important consideration.
36. Micro-Irrigation

Micro-irrigation supplies water in controlled quantities.

Major types:

  • Drip irrigation.
  • Sprinkler irrigation.
37. Drip Irrigation
  • Water is delivered directly near the root zone through pipes and emitters.
  • It reduces evaporation and runoff.
📌 Must-Memorise

Drip → Root-Zone Water Supply

38. Advantages of Drip Irrigation
  • Saves water.
  • Reduces weed growth.
  • Improves fertiliser-use efficiency.
  • Suitable for orchards.
  • Useful for water-scarce regions.
39. Crops Suitable for Drip Irrigation

Common examples include:

  • Sugarcane.
  • Banana.
  • Coconut.
  • Grapes.
  • Vegetables.
  • Fruit crops.
40. Fertigation
  • Fertigation means applying soluble fertilisers through irrigation water.
  • It is commonly associated with drip systems.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fertigation → Fertiliser + Irrigation

41. Sprinkler Irrigation
  • Water is sprayed over crops through nozzles.
  • It resembles artificial rainfall.
42. Areas Suitable for Sprinklers

Sprinkler irrigation is useful in:

  • Sandy soils.
  • Uneven terrain.
  • Water-scarce areas.
  • Light-textured soils.
43. Drip vs Sprinkler

Drip:

  • Direct to root zone.
  • Very high water-use efficiency.
  • Best for row crops, orchards and plantations.

Sprinkler:

  • Sprays over field.
  • Useful for larger field coverage and uneven terrain.
44. Flood Irrigation
  • Flood irrigation spreads water across the field surface.
  • It is simple but may waste large amounts of water.
45. Furrow Irrigation
  • Water moves through small channels between crop rows.
  • It is useful for row crops.
46. Basin Irrigation
  • Water is retained within small level basins.
  • It is commonly used for:
  • Orchards.
  • Paddy in modified forms.
47. Irrigation Efficiency
  • Irrigation efficiency measures how effectively supplied water is used by crops.
  • Water may be lost through:
  • Evaporation.
  • Seepage.
  • Runoff.
  • Deep percolation.
48. Conveyance Efficiency
  • Conveyance efficiency refers to the proportion of diverted water that reaches the farm.
  • Canal lining can reduce seepage losses.
49. Canal Lining
  • Canal lining involves covering canal beds and sides with impermeable material.
  • It reduces seepage.
50. Field Application Efficiency
  • Field application efficiency indicates how much delivered water remains available in the crop root zone.
51. Water-Use Efficiency
  • Water-use efficiency broadly refers to agricultural output obtained per unit of water used.
  • It is especially important in dry regions.
52. Irrigation Scheduling
  • Irrigation scheduling decides:
  • When to irrigate.
  • How much water to apply.
  • Proper scheduling prevents both moisture stress and over-irrigation.
53. Critical Irrigation Stage
  • Different crops are especially sensitive to water shortage at certain growth stages.
  • Irrigation during these stages can strongly influence yield.
54. Irrigation and Rice
  • Paddy is one of India's major irrigation-demanding crops.
  • Continuous flooding is not essential throughout the entire crop cycle, but sufficient soil moisture is critical.
55. Irrigation and Wheat
  • Wheat requires irrigation especially in areas with limited winter rainfall.
  • Proper irrigation at critical growth stages improves yield.
56. Irrigation and Sugarcane
  • Sugarcane has high water demand because of:
  • Long growing duration.
  • High biomass production.
  • Drip irrigation can reduce water use.
57. Irrigation and Cotton
  • Cotton requires moisture during growth but dry weather during boll opening.
  • Excess irrigation can harm the crop.
58. Irrigation and Horticulture

Reliable irrigation supports:

  • Banana.
  • Grapes.
  • Citrus.
  • Vegetables.
  • Flowers.
  • Plantation crops.
59. Irrigation and Crop Diversification
  • Irrigation can enable farmers to shift toward:
  • Vegetables.
  • Fruits.
  • Sugarcane.
  • Fodder.
  • Multiple crops.
  • However, crop choice should match local water availability.
60. Multipurpose River-Valley Projects

Such projects may provide:

  • Irrigation.
  • Hydroelectric power.
  • Flood control.
  • Drinking water.
  • Navigation.
  • Fisheries.
61. Dam
  • A dam is a barrier constructed across a river or valley to store or regulate water.
62. Reservoir
  • A reservoir is the water body created or enlarged by a dam or storage structure.
63. Barrage
  • A barrage is a gated structure built across a river mainly to regulate and divert water.
  • Unlike a large storage dam, its principal function is often diversion.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Dam → Mainly Storage

Barrage → Mainly Regulation/Diversion

64. Weir
  • A weir is a low barrier built across a river to raise water level and divert flow.
  • Kallanai is a famous ancient diversion structure.
65. Bhakra-Nangal Project
  • Bhakra Dam is built on the Sutlej River.
  • It supports:
  • Irrigation.
  • Hydroelectricity.
  • It benefits northwestern India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhakra → Sutlej

66. Hirakud Project
  • Hirakud Dam is built on the Mahanadi in Odisha.
  • Major purposes include:
  • Irrigation.
  • Flood moderation.
  • Hydropower.
📌 Must-Memorise

Hirakud → Mahanadi

67. Damodar Valley Project
  • Damodar Valley development was designed for:
  • Flood control.
  • Irrigation.
  • Power generation.
  • Damodar was historically called the Sorrow of Bengal.
68. Nagarjuna Sagar
  • Nagarjuna Sagar is built on the Krishna River.
  • It supports irrigation and power generation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nagarjuna Sagar → Krishna

69. Sardar Sarovar
  • Sardar Sarovar is built on the Narmada River.
  • It provides irrigation and water supply to dry regions.
70. Tungabhadra Project
  • Tungabhadra project is associated with the Tungabhadra River.
  • It supports irrigation in parts of Karnataka and adjoining regions.
71. Tehri Project
  • Tehri Dam is built on the Bhagirathi.
  • It is used for:
  • Hydropower.
  • Irrigation-related regulation.
  • Water supply.
72. Indira Gandhi Canal
  • Indira Gandhi Canal is one of India's major canal-irrigation projects.
  • It carries water to the dry regions of Rajasthan.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indira Gandhi Canal → Rajasthan Desert Irrigation

73. Source of Indira Gandhi Canal
  • The canal receives water from the Sutlej-Beas river system through the Harike headworks region.
74. Impact of Indira Gandhi Canal

Positive impacts include:

  • Irrigated agriculture.
  • Settlement expansion.
  • Increased crop production.

Potential problems include:

  • Waterlogging.
  • Salinity.
  • Ecological change.
75. Kallanai / Grand Anicut
  • Kallanai is an ancient diversion structure across the Kaveri.
  • It is traditionally associated with Karikala Chola.
  • It lies near Tiruchirappalli.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Kallanai → Kaveri → Karikala Chola

76. Purpose of Kallanai
  • Kallanai diverts Kaveri water into irrigation channels.
  • It supports agriculture in the Kaveri delta.
77. Mettur Dam
  • Mettur Dam is built on Kaveri in Tamil Nadu.
  • Its reservoir is called Stanley Reservoir.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Mettur → Kaveri → Stanley Reservoir

78. Mettur and Kaveri Delta Irrigation
  • Water released from Mettur supports irrigation in downstream Kaveri delta districts.
  • Timing of release is especially important for paddy cultivation.
79. Bhavanisagar Dam
  • Bhavanisagar Dam is built on the Bhavani River.
  • It is also associated with the Lower Bhavani Project.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Bhavanisagar → Bhavani

80. Lower Bhavani Project
  • It is an important irrigation system of western Tamil Nadu.
  • It supports agriculture in the Erode region and adjoining areas.
81. Amaravathi Dam
  • Amaravathi Dam is built on the Amaravati River.
  • It supports irrigation in western Tamil Nadu.
82. Vaigai Dam
  • Vaigai Dam is built on the Vaigai River.
  • It supports irrigation and water supply in southern Tamil Nadu.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Vaigai Dam → Vaigai

83. Mullaperiyar Project
  • Mullaperiyar Dam is built across the Periyar River in Kerala.
  • Water is diverted eastward toward Tamil Nadu.
  • It supports agriculture in the Vaigai basin and adjoining southern districts.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Mullaperiyar → Periyar Water Diverted to Tamil Nadu

84. Papanasam Project
  • Papanasam Dam is associated with the Tamiraparani river system.
  • It supports irrigation and hydroelectricity.
85. Manimuthar Dam
  • Manimuthar Dam is built on the Manimuthar River.
  • It supports irrigation in southern Tamil Nadu.
86. Sathanur Dam
  • Sathanur Dam is built across the Thenpennai/Ponnaiyar river system.
  • It is an important irrigation project in northern Tamil Nadu.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Sathanur → South Pennar/Ponnaiyar System

87. Krishnagiri Reservoir Project
  • Krishnagiri reservoir is associated with the Ponnaiyar river system.
  • It supports irrigation in northern Tamil Nadu.
88. Aliyar Project
  • Aliyar Dam is located in western Tamil Nadu.
  • It forms part of an important irrigation and water-transfer system.
89. Parambikulam-Aliyar Project
  • Parambikulam-Aliyar is an inter-basin water-development project involving Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
  • It transfers and regulates water across several west-flowing and east-flowing streams.
  • It supports irrigation in western Tamil Nadu.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

PAP → Parambikulam-Aliyar → Western Tamil Nadu Irrigation

90. Parambikulam-Aliyar Benefits

It supports agriculture in:

  • Coimbatore region.
  • Tiruppur region.
  • Pollachi belt and adjoining areas.
91. Pollachi Agriculture and Irrigation

Reliable irrigation supports:

  • Coconut.
  • Banana.
  • Fodder.
  • Vegetables.
  • Other commercial crops.
92. Periyar-Vaigai Link
  • Water diverted from Periyar contributes to the Vaigai irrigation system.
  • This demonstrates inter-basin transfer.
93. Inter-Basin Water Transfer
  • Inter-basin transfer moves water from one drainage basin to another.
  • It is used where water availability and demand differ spatially.
94. Benefits of Inter-Basin Transfer

Potential benefits include:

  • Irrigation.
  • Drinking water.
  • Drought relief.
  • Regional water balancing.
95. Concerns with Inter-Basin Transfer

Possible concerns include:

  • Ecological change.
  • Altered river flow.
  • Displacement.
  • Interstate disputes.
  • High construction cost.
96. Command Area
  • Command area is the geographical area that can receive irrigation from a canal or project.
📌 Must-Memorise

Command Area → Area Served by Irrigation Project

97. Cultivable Command Area
  • Cultivable command area is the portion of a command area that is suitable for cultivation.
98. Command Area Development

It aims to improve:

  • Water distribution.
  • Drainage.
  • Field channels.
  • Land levelling.
  • Agricultural productivity.
99. Warabandi
  • Warabandi is a rotational system of distributing canal water among farmers according to a fixed schedule.
  • It is commonly associated with northwestern canal-irrigation systems.
📌 TNPSC Advanced Fact

Warabandi → Rotational Canal Water Distribution

100. Water Users Association
  • Water Users Associations involve farmers in local irrigation management.
  • They can assist with:
  • Water distribution.
  • Maintenance.
  • Conflict reduction.
101. Participatory Irrigation Management
  • Participatory irrigation management involves users in planning and management of irrigation systems.
  • It aims to improve efficiency and accountability.
102. Tank User Participation
  • Community participation is especially important in maintaining:
  • Tank bunds.
  • Supply channels.
  • Surplus channels.
  • Sluices.
103. Kudimaramathu
  • Kudimaramathu traditionally refers to community participation in maintenance of irrigation tanks and water structures in Tamil Nadu.
  • It has historical importance in local water management.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Kudimaramathu → Community Tank Maintenance

104. Tank Sluice
  • A sluice is a controlled opening used to release stored tank water into irrigation channels.
105. Tank Bund
  • A bund is an embankment that retains water in a tank.
  • Breach of a bund can cause flooding and loss of stored water.
106. Surplus Weir
  • A surplus weir safely releases excess tank water when storage exceeds capacity.
  • It protects the bund from overtopping.
107. Field Channel
  • Field channels carry irrigation water from the main distribution system to individual fields.
108. Irrigation Duty
  • Irrigation duty refers to the area that can be irrigated by a unit discharge of water during a crop period.
  • It is an engineering measure of water use.
109. Delta of a Crop — Irrigation Term
  • In irrigation engineering, delta means the total depth of water required by a crop during its base period.
  • It should not be confused with a river delta.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Irrigation Delta ≠ River Delta

110. Base Period
  • Base period is the time between the first and last irrigation required for a crop.
111. Consumptive Use of Water
  • Consumptive use includes water lost mainly through:
  • Evaporation.
  • Transpiration.
  • It represents water actually consumed in crop production.
112. Evapotranspiration
  • Evapotranspiration is the combined loss of water through:
  • Evaporation.
  • Plant transpiration.
📌 Must-Memorise

Evapotranspiration = Evaporation + Transpiration

113. Soil-Moisture Conservation

Important methods include:

  • Mulching.
  • Contour bunding.
  • Reduced tillage.
  • Farm ponds.
  • Crop residue retention.
114. Rainwater Harvesting for Agriculture

Rainwater can be stored using:

  • Farm ponds.
  • Check dams.
  • Tanks.
  • Percolation ponds.
115. Farm Pond
  • A farm pond stores rainfall runoff for:
  • Supplemental irrigation.
  • Livestock.
  • Aquaculture in some cases.
116. Check Dam
  • Check dams slow stream flow.
  • They help:
  • Recharge groundwater.
  • Trap sediment.
  • Store limited water.
117. Percolation Pond
  • A percolation pond is designed mainly to increase groundwater recharge.
  • Stored water infiltrates into the ground.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Percolation Pond → Groundwater Recharge

118. Watershed Development

Watershed development integrates:

  • Soil conservation.
  • Water harvesting.
  • Vegetation management.
  • Agricultural improvement.
119. Watershed Approach
  • The entire drainage area is treated as one planning unit.
  • Activities are usually planned from upper slopes toward lower areas.
120. Contour Bunding
  • Bunds are constructed along contour lines.
  • They reduce runoff and erosion.
121. Gully Plugging
  • Small barriers are placed across gullies.
  • They slow runoff and trap soil.
122. Agricultural Development — Meaning

Agricultural development involves improvement in:

  • Productivity.
  • Irrigation.
  • Technology.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Crop diversification.
  • Farmer income.
  • Sustainability.
123. Agricultural Productivity
  • Productivity means agricultural output per unit of land or another input.
  • Yield per hectare is a common measure.
124. Production vs Productivity

Production:

  • Total quantity produced.

Productivity:

  • Output per unit area.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

High Production ≠ Necessarily High Productivity

125. Green Revolution and Irrigation
  • Irrigation was a critical component of the Green Revolution.
  • HYV seeds performed best with reliable water and fertiliser supply.
126. Green Revolution Regions

Early gains were strongest in:

  • Punjab.
  • Haryana.
  • Western Uttar Pradesh.

because irrigation infrastructure was well developed.

127. Agricultural Mechanisation

Mechanisation includes:

  • Tractors.
  • Harvesters.
  • Pumps.
  • Seed drills.
  • Threshers.
128. Mechanisation and Irrigation

Electric and diesel pumps greatly expanded groundwater irrigation in India.

129. Rural Electrification and Agriculture

Electricity supports:

  • Irrigation pumps.
  • Cold storage.
  • Processing.
  • Farm machinery.
130. Fertilisers and Irrigation
  • Fertilisers are more effective when adequate soil moisture is available.
  • This is why irrigation and fertiliser use often expand together.
131. Agricultural Extension
  • Agricultural extension provides farmers with information on:
  • Crops.
  • Irrigation.
  • Pests.
  • Weather.
  • Technology.
132. Precision Irrigation

Precision systems may use:

  • Soil-moisture sensors.
  • Automated valves.
  • Weather data.
  • Drip systems.

They apply water according to crop need.

133. Soil-Moisture Sensor
  • Soil-moisture sensors indicate water availability in the root zone.
  • They help prevent unnecessary irrigation.
134. Remote Sensing in Irrigation

Satellite imagery helps monitor:

  • Irrigated area.
  • Crop condition.
  • Reservoir extent.
  • Drought.
135. GIS in Irrigation Planning

GIS helps map:

  • Canals.
  • Command areas.
  • Tanks.
  • Groundwater zones.
  • Crop-water demand.
136. Agricultural Development and Roads

Better rural roads improve:

  • Input supply.
  • Market access.
  • Transport of perishables.
  • Farm-gate prices.
137. Agricultural Storage

Storage infrastructure protects crops from:

  • Moisture.
  • Insects.
  • Rodents.
  • Spoilage.
138. Cold Chain
  • Cold chains are important for:
  • Fruits.
  • Vegetables.
  • Milk.
  • Fish.
  • They reduce post-harvest losses.
139. Agro-Processing

Irrigation-supported crop production can encourage:

  • Sugar mills.
  • Rice mills.
  • Cotton processing.
  • Fruit processing.
  • Dairy industries.
140. Agricultural Diversification

Diversification into:

  • Horticulture.
  • Livestock.
  • Fisheries.
  • Pulses.
  • Oilseeds.

can improve resilience and income.

141. Irrigation and Water-Intensive Crops

High irrigation availability may encourage:

  • Paddy.
  • Sugarcane.
  • Banana.

If water supply is unsustainable, these crops can create stress.

142. Crop-Water Matching
  • Crop choice should match local water availability.
  • Dry regions are better suited to less water-demanding crops unless reliable irrigation exists.
143. Millets and Irrigation
  • Millets generally require less irrigation than paddy.
  • They are well suited to rainfed drylands.
144. Pulses and Water Use
  • Many pulse crops require less water than rice or sugarcane.
  • They can also improve soil nitrogen.
145. Groundnut and Irrigation
  • Groundnut requires well-drained soil.
  • Excess irrigation and waterlogging are harmful.
146. Water Productivity
  • Water productivity refers to crop output or economic value produced per unit of water.
  • It is an important measure in water-scarce agriculture.
147. Virtual Water — Agricultural Link
  • Virtual water is water embedded in producing a commodity.
  • Water-intensive agricultural products contain a high virtual-water requirement.
148. Irrigation and Groundwater Recharge
  • Irrigation return flow can recharge groundwater.
  • However, excessive surface irrigation may also cause waterlogging and salinity.
149. Conjunctive Use
  • Conjunctive use means coordinated use of surface water and groundwater.
  • It can improve water reliability and help manage waterlogging.
📌 TNPSC Advanced Fact

Conjunctive Use → Surface Water + Groundwater

150. Managed Aquifer Recharge
  • Managed aquifer recharge deliberately increases groundwater storage.
  • Methods include:
  • Recharge wells.
  • Percolation ponds.
  • Check dams.
151. Rainfed Agriculture Development

Important measures include:

  • Watershed development.
  • Drought-resistant seeds.
  • Farm ponds.
  • Soil-moisture conservation.
  • Crop diversification.
152. Dryland Agriculture Development

Dryland farming can be improved through:

  • Contour farming.
  • Mulching.
  • Millets.
  • Pulses.
  • Water harvesting.
  • Short-duration varieties.
153. Irrigation and Food Security

Reliable irrigation:

  • Stabilises food production.
  • Supports Rabi crops.
  • Reduces drought-related crop failure.
154. Irrigation and Regional Inequality

Regions with reliable irrigation often achieve:

  • Higher productivity.
  • More crop cycles.
  • Greater commercialisation.

Rainfed regions may lag without suitable development support.

155. Irrigation-Induced Environmental Problems

Potential problems include:

  • Waterlogging.
  • Salinity.
  • Groundwater depletion.
  • River-flow reduction.
  • Wetland alteration.
  • Agrochemical runoff.
156. Dam Sedimentation
  • Reservoirs gradually accumulate sediment.
  • This reduces storage capacity.
  • Catchment erosion accelerates sedimentation.
157. Irrigation Reservoir Evaporation
  • Large reservoirs lose water through evaporation.
  • Loss is greater in hot, dry climates.
158. Canal Seepage

Canal seepage can:

Benefit:

  • Recharge groundwater.

Problem:

  • Cause waterlogging where drainage is poor.
159. Agricultural Drainage
  • Drainage removes excess water from fields.
  • It is essential in heavily irrigated regions.
160. Surface Drainage
  • Surface drainage removes excess water from the land surface through channels.
161. Subsurface Drainage
  • Subsurface drains remove excess water below the soil surface.
  • They can help reclaim waterlogged and saline lands.
162. Water Harvesting and Climate Variability
  • Local storage improves resilience to:
  • Dry spells.
  • Delayed monsoon.
  • Short droughts.
163. Irrigation and Climate Change

Potential challenges include:

  • Higher evaporation.
  • Changing rainfall.
  • Glacier-flow changes.
  • More droughts.
  • Greater competition for water.
164. Efficient Irrigation as Adaptation

Efficient irrigation reduces vulnerability by:

  • Saving water.
  • Stabilising crops.
  • Reducing pumping demand.
  • Supporting drought management.
165. Tamil Nadu Irrigation Geography — Overview

Tamil Nadu depends on:

  • Rivers.
  • Reservoirs.
  • Tanks.
  • Wells.
  • Borewells.
  • Inter-basin transfers.
  • Northeast monsoon rainfall.
166. Why Irrigation is Crucial in Tamil Nadu

Reasons include:

  • Limited perennial rivers.
  • High rainfall variability.
  • Strong northeast monsoon dependence.
  • Large dry interior areas.
  • High agricultural demand.
167. Kaveri Irrigation System

Major elements include:

  • Mettur Reservoir.
  • Kallanai.
  • Canal networks.
  • Kollidam system.
  • Delta distributaries.
168. Kaveri Delta Irrigation

Kaveri water supports:

  • Kuruvai.
  • Samba.
  • Thaladi.
  • Sugarcane.
  • Banana.
  • Pulses in crop rotations.
169. Mettur Release and Kuruvai
  • Kuruvai paddy depends strongly on timely water availability from the Kaveri system.
  • Delayed water supply can reduce the cultivated area.
170. Northeast Monsoon and Tanks
  • October-December rainfall fills many Tamil Nadu tanks.
  • Tank storage supports subsequent cultivation.
171. Vaigai Basin Irrigation

Water sources include:

  • Vaigai Dam.
  • Periyar diversion.
  • Tanks.
  • Groundwater.
172. Tamiraparani Irrigation
  • Tamiraparani has comparatively dependable flow.
  • It supports paddy, banana and other crops in southern Tamil Nadu.
173. Palar Basin Irrigation
  • Palar is highly seasonal.
  • Agriculture relies substantially on:
  • Groundwater.
  • Tanks.
  • Seasonal runoff.
174. Ponnaiyar Basin Irrigation

Important structures include:

  • Sathanur Dam.
  • Krishnagiri reservoir.
  • Tanks and groundwater systems.
175. Western Tamil Nadu Irrigation

Important sources include:

  • Bhavanisagar.
  • Parambikulam-Aliyar system.
  • Amaravathi.
  • Wells and borewells.
176. Bhavani Basin Agriculture

Irrigation supports:

  • Paddy.
  • Sugarcane.
  • Turmeric.
  • Banana.
  • Other commercial crops.
177. Pollachi Irrigation
  • Parambikulam-Aliyar water and groundwater support intensive coconut cultivation.
  • The region is one of Tamil Nadu's best-known coconut belts.
178. Southern Tamil Nadu Irrigation

Important systems include:

  • Vaigai.
  • Mullaperiyar transfer.
  • Tamiraparani.
  • Manimuthar.
  • Tanks.
179. Coastal Tamil Nadu Irrigation Challenges

Problems include:

  • Seawater intrusion.
  • Salinity.
  • Cyclone flooding.
  • Groundwater over-extraction.
180. Groundwater and Tamil Nadu Agriculture

Groundwater is especially important for:

  • Coconut.
  • Banana.
  • Sugarcane.
  • Vegetables.
  • Dry-season cultivation.
181. Borewell Dependence
  • Borewell irrigation provides flexible water access.
  • Excessive drilling can lead to declining aquifers.
182. Hard-Rock Aquifers in Tamil Nadu
  • Much of Tamil Nadu has crystalline hard-rock geology.
  • Groundwater is stored mainly in:
  • Weathered zones.
  • Fractures.
  • Storage is generally more limited than in thick alluvial aquifers.

TN Groundwater → Hard-Rock Fracture Aquifers

183. Tank-Groundwater Link
  • Tanks recharge nearby wells.
  • Loss of tank storage can reduce groundwater recharge.
184. Cascade Tanks and Flood Control
  • Tank cascades intercept runoff at multiple levels.
  • They reduce sudden downstream flows.
  • They also store water for agriculture.
185. Desilting Supply Channels
  • Removing silt and vegetation from supply channels improves inflow into tanks.
186. Protecting Tank Catchments
  • Encroachment or construction in tank catchments reduces inflow.
  • Catchment protection is therefore essential.
187. Micro-Irrigation in Tamil Nadu

Drip irrigation is particularly useful for:

  • Sugarcane.
  • Coconut.
  • Banana.
  • Mango.
  • Grapes.
  • Vegetables.
188. Theni and Drip Irrigation
  • Drip systems are suitable for grape and fruit cultivation in water-limited regions such as Theni.
189. Western TN and Drip Irrigation
  • Coconut, banana and horticulture in western Tamil Nadu can benefit from drip systems.
190. Agricultural Development in Tamil Nadu

Important geographical components include:

  • Irrigation modernisation.
  • Tank restoration.
  • Micro-irrigation.
  • Crop diversification.
  • Horticulture.
  • Water harvesting.
  • Soil conservation.
191. TNPSC High-Yield Dam–River Pairings
  • Bhakra → Sutlej.
  • Hirakud → Mahanadi.
  • Nagarjuna Sagar → Krishna.
  • Sardar Sarovar → Narmada.
  • Tehri → Bhagirathi.
  • Mettur → Kaveri.
  • Bhavanisagar → Bhavani.
  • Vaigai Dam → Vaigai.
  • Sathanur → Ponnaiyar.
  • Manimuthar → Manimuthar.
  • Papanasam → Tamiraparani system.
192. Tamil Nadu High-Yield Irrigation Pairings
  • Kallanai → Kaveri.
  • Mettur → Stanley Reservoir.
  • Bhavanisagar → Lower Bhavani.
  • Mullaperiyar → Periyar diversion.
  • Parambikulam-Aliyar → Western Tamil Nadu.
  • Sathanur → Ponnaiyar.
  • Vaigai Dam → Southern TN.
  • Kudimaramathu → Tank maintenance.
  • Eri → Tank irrigation.
  • Kuruvai → Kaveri irrigation.
193. TNPSC Traps
  • Irrigation supplements rainfall; it does not replace climate.
  • Canal irrigation is best suited to relatively level terrain.
  • Inundation canals and perennial canals are different.
  • Tube wells are particularly suitable in alluvial aquifers.
  • Excess groundwater pumping lowers the water table.
  • Tank irrigation is especially important in Peninsular India.
  • Tamil Nadu's traditional tanks are called eris.
  • Drip irrigation supplies water near roots.
  • Sprinkler irrigation resembles artificial rainfall.
  • Fertigation means fertiliser application through irrigation.
  • Over-irrigation can cause both salinity and waterlogging.
  • Dam and barrage are not exactly the same.
  • Kallanai is primarily a diversion structure.
  • Mettur is on Kaveri.
  • Bhavanisagar is on Bhavani.
  • Mullaperiyar diverts Periyar water eastward toward Tamil Nadu.
  • Parambikulam-Aliyar is an inter-basin project.
  • Indira Gandhi Canal irrigates Rajasthan.
  • Command area means land served by an irrigation system.
  • Warabandi means rotational canal-water distribution.
  • Evapotranspiration combines evaporation and transpiration.
  • Percolation ponds mainly promote groundwater recharge.
  • Conjunctive use means coordinated use of surface and groundwater.
  • Irrigation delta is not a river delta.
  • High irrigation does not automatically mean sustainable agriculture.
  • Water-intensive crops can create groundwater stress.
  • Tamil Nadu's tanks also support recharge and flood moderation.

  • PAP → Western TN.
  • Sathanur → Ponnaiyar.
  • Kudimaramathu → Tank maintenance.
  • Command area → Irrigated service area.
  • Warabandi → Rotational supply.
  • Evapotranspiration → E + T.
  • Percolation pond → Recharge.
